title: Whether each approval decision reaches exactly the tool call it was issued for, when a step's tool call ids repeat
pins: The pairing of a person's approval decision with the one tool call it was issued for. A decision reaches a call through the tool call id its approval request names, and a provider can return two calls in one step under the same id, or under an empty id. Drift here does not error: a step that paired decisions by id could run a call nobody approved, or run one call twice on one approval. When a step's tool call ids repeat (empty ids count) no gated call in that step may run, whatever was decided, and no later decision or resume may revive one; a step whose ids are distinct is decided call by call. In every language.
scope: One model step with two or three calls to a gated tool `echo`, with distinct ids, one shared id, empty ids, or a shared id on two of three calls; an ungated tool `free` sharing the gated calls' id; decisions in every order, all at once or one round at a time. Each language's runtime is driven at its public seam, offline with a fake model: PHP through Prism's OpenAI Responses handler over faked HTTP with Session::decide(), TypeScript with recordDecisions(), Python with record_approval() once per decision, since it has no batch call. Not in these rows: approval requests that repeat a tool_call_id while the calls do not (that shape only arises from a stored row another writer produced, so it is pinned by each language's own tests), streamed decisions, plan-held and subagent steps, and the denial reason text, which each language's own tests pin.
findings: All eleven rows agree in all three languages, and that agreement is a statement about the rule each runner was written against, not proof the rule is right. Every expectation was written before any language ran and committed before any result was recorded. The rows were probed against each harness at the commit before its G-392 change: rows apr-0004, apr-0006, apr-0007 and apr-0008 fail in all three languages there, and the distinct-id controls apr-0001 to apr-0003 pass, so the suite separates the rule from a runtime that pairs decisions by id. Rows apr-0005, apr-0009, apr-0010 and apr-0011 also passed before the change, so they pin the outcome without discriminating it. No row needed a language-specific skip: every language accepted an empty tool call id from its fake client.
